title: How to use AI as a student
description: Understand difficult material, gather sources that hold up to scrutiny, strengthen your own drafts, and keep track of a whole term.
introduction: Student work is mostly research and production under a deadline. The reading you have bounced off three times, the sources that need to hold up when a marker checks them, the essay and the group project and the form that all land in the same week. That's where the time actually goes.

Most AI tools offer to write the essay, which is the part you're meant to do. Strawberry works in the browser instead, so it can follow a reading list into the databases and journals your institution already gives you access to, compare what it finds against your own course material, and keep the link and date next to every claim. What comes back is something you can check and build on.

sections.title: What Strawberry can help you do

items.title: Understand the material
items.description: Get a hard topic explained at the level you actually need, against your own readings.

items.title: Find sources that hold up
items.description: Gather current, credible sources with links and dates you can cite and defend.

items.title: Strengthen what you have written
items.description: Pressure-test your own argument, structure, and evidence, and present finished work well.

items.title: Stay ahead of the term
items.description: See what needs attention today and catch the commitments you have forgotten.

blocks.text: Not sure where to start? Tell your companion what's due and when, and it can suggest the most useful thing to do first.

skill.context: Help me work out where to start with what I have due.

blocks.text: Being stuck on a reading is rarely about vocabulary. Usually a paper assumes a debate you haven't met yet, and no amount of rereading the paragraph will supply it. What helps is someone mapping the argument around it. Which position is this author writing against, and why did it matter enough to publish?

Your companion can explain the topic at the level you actually need and work from your own set readings rather than a generic summary, which matters when a popular explanation online quietly contradicts what your course expects you to know.

items.context: Map this field so I can see the main positions and who is worth reading.

blocks.text: A citation is a promise that someone else can go and check. That's why invented references do so much damage, and why a source you haven't opened is a liability rather than an asset.

Strawberry can work through the library databases, journal subscriptions, and reading lists you are already entitled to use, then bring what it finds together with the open web. It keeps the link and the date beside each claim, separates what a source actually says from an interpretation of it, and flags where two credible sources disagree instead of quietly picking one.
That last part is worth more than it sounds. A genuine disagreement between two respected sources is usually a better paragraph than another citation that agrees with you.

items.context: Collect these fields across the papers or records I need into one clean table.
Research this organization before my application or interview.

blocks.text: Strawberry won't write an assessed submission for you, or invent a quotation to fill a gap. It will pressure-test an outline that doesn't hold, find evidence where your argument is thin, name the counterargument you have avoided, and give honest feedback on a draft you wrote. That's supervisor work, and most students get far too little of it.

items.context: Turn my finished work into a presentation I can actually present.

blocks.text: Deadlines rarely fail because the work was too hard. They fail because a reading, a form, a supervisor's email, and a group project all came due in the same week and nothing was tracking them together.

items.title: See today clearly
items.text: What deserves your attention now, across deadlines, calendar, and messages.

skill.context: Show me what deserves my attention today.

items.title: Catch what you have forgotten
items.text: The commitments, unanswered emails, and follow-ups that have gone quiet.

skill.context: Find the commitments and replies I still owe.

blocks.text: Once a way of working proves useful, it can be saved. Your citation style, the sources you trust, how you like feedback delivered. The next essay starts from there instead of a blank page. If something genuinely recurs, like watching a journal or a funding call for new material, it can become a Routine.
